title: Ocean warming weakens the sea–land breeze in coastal megacities
abstract: The sea–land breeze (SLB), driven by thermal contrasts between sea and land, forms a key circulation system in coastal cities which mitigates urban heat islands, improves air quality and supports urban liveability. Yet its response to rising sea-surface temperatures (SST) under global warming remains unclear. Here we simulate SLB evolution across 18 major coastal megacities under varying SST. The results show that historical SST increases have reduced SLB days by 3–45% in 67% of these cities, with mid-latitude cities experiencing the largest declines (29–45%) as a result of a more than 5% reduction in diurnal sea–land thermal contrast. A further 0.52 °C (~2%) SST increase relative to historical levels induces a 4.5-fold reduction in SLB days in high-impact regions and heightened sensitivity in moderate-impact regions under high-emission scenarios. This erosion of SLB days, primarily driven by ocean warming, poses a critical yet overlooked threat to coastal liveability. The sea–land breeze acts to counter urban heat in many coastal cities. Here the authors simulate how this circulation changes with warming ocean water, showing that it decreases in most of them, adding heat stress to urban areas.
problem: The response of the sea-land breeze, a critical circulation system for coastal city liveability, to rising sea-surface temperatures under global warming remains unclear, obscuring an overlooked threat to urban thermal comfort and air quality.
method: The study simulates sea-land breeze changes in 18 coastal megacities by integrating dynamic, high-resolution sea-surface temperature data from global climate models into a regional weather model to assess the impact of historical and future ocean warming under various emission scenarios.
task: The task is to simulate the evolution of the sea-land breeze (SLB) across 18 major coastal megacities to quantify how rising sea-surface temperatures under historical and future global warming scenarios weaken this critical atmospheric circulation system.

Enhanced evaporation due to increased SST raises atmospheric moisture, resulting in more frequent heavy rainfall and urban flooding. Increased SST leads to a rising occurrence of intense typhoons causing severe damage to urban areas.

Climbing SST exacerbates the urban heat island effect, especially in summer. The heat from the warming ocean combined with anthropogenic heat from urban areas further amplifies extreme heat events

High-resolution SST data from the CMIP6 (BCC-CSM2-MR model, 0.3°–1° spatial resolution from the equator towards the poles) has been used in this research.

Another four high-resolution SST datasets from CMIP6 were used in this study, namely ACCESS-ESM1.5 (~1.25° × 1.875°), CanESM5 (~2.8° × 2.8°), CESM2 (~1.25° × 0.9°) and EC-Earth3 (~1.0° × 1.0°), to evaluate how intermodel differences in SST affect the simulation outcomes.
